summary: Vermilion Light at the Lake Erie pier mouth: wooden beacon 1847, iron tower 1877, skeletal tower 1929, 1992 replica tower, relit 2016 under the City of Vermilion.

light.characteristic: fixed red (from 1880 per LighthouseFriends); 1919 acetylene conversion gave a white flash every three seconds (LighthouseFriends); current characteristic per 2016 Light List as reported by LighthouseFriends is fixed red

lens.note: Original 1877 fifth-order Barbier and Fenestre lens; the 1992 replica used a museum fifth-order lens; a fifth-order replica lens was installed September 2016 (Main Street Vermilion).

structures.status: removed 1929; renovated and moved to Lake Ontario as East Charity Shoal Light (1935)

structures.note: Ten-foot tower (LighthouseFriends); height disputed (Wikipedia gives 18 ft; not cited in story).

structures.type: octagonal replica of the 1877 iron tower
structures.status: active aid to navigation since 2016 relight
structures.note: Built 1991-92 (groundbreaking 24 July 1991; raised 23 October 1991; dedicated 6 June 1992). Height disputed: LighthouseFriends calls it a sixteen-foot replica in one place; Wikipedia says 34 ft.
Dwelling on the corner of Liberty and Grand Streets bought by the government in 1871; now in commercial use (LighthouseFriends).

staffing.note: Acetylene conversion 1919; light placed under the Lorain keepers (LighthouseFriends). A lighthouse keeper was appointed in 2016 (Main Street Vermilion).

access.note: Grounds open; visitors welcome at any time; interior closed (Main Street Vermilion; LighthouseFriends).

facts.ownership: City of Vermilion (site transferred 2014; museum closed); lighthouse, propeller and anchor under city care (Main Street Vermilion).
facts.agency: City of Vermilion; listed by the Coast Guard as a museum light, fixed red (2016 Light List, per LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Congress appropriates $3,000 for a beacon light and head of pier; wooden beacon (LighthouseFriends; archive year established 1847).
Beacon light and pier rebuilt for $5,000; whale-oil lamp with a sixth-order lens.
Government purchases a house on a lot near the piers as the keeper's dwelling; altered for oil storage (LighthouseFriends).
Iron tower raised at the end of the pier in September 1877; 34 ft high; 5th-order Barbier and Fenestre Fresnel lens; 400-foot catwalk to shore.
From fixed white to fixed red (LighthouseFriends).
27 April 1893: schooner M. S. Bacon, under tow from the tug J. P. Devney, struck the light-tower on the west pier; two angle-iron plates damaged.
Oil shed for 540 gallons built south of the light; 500-foot elevated iron walk built on the pier (LighthouseFriends).

Lamp converted to acetylene, 2 September 1919 (LighthouseFriends); Bulletin 1919 illuminant-change list (page image): Vermilion, Ohio, oil to acetylene, fixed red to flashing white; index lists change in illuminant at Vermillion (p.95).
Characteristic changed to a white flash every three seconds (LighthouseFriends).
Keeper's house sold to the local Masonic Lodge in the early 1920s (LighthouseFriends).
Iron tower found leaning after an icy storm undermined the pier; dismantled and removed in March 1929; cast-iron pieces hauled away (LighthouseFriends).
Skeletal steel tower erected to mark the pier; moved to outer end of west pier 5 October 1929 (LighthouseFriends).
Electric fixed-red range lights established on the pier, the skeletal tower as front light (LighthouseFriends).
Iron tower renovated and set on a cement crib off Cape Vincent as East Charity Shoal Light (LighthouseFriends).
Replica tower built 1991 (groundbreaking 24 July 1991; raised 23 October 1991); dedicated 6 June 1992; funds of $55,000 raised by local campaign.
Replica lit after dedication (fifth-order lens from the museum).
Former Inland Seas museum site and parcel transferred to the City of Vermilion (LighthouseFriends).
Fifth-order replica lens installed (September 2016); relighting ceremony 15 September 2016; active navigational aid (Main Street Vermilion).

corrections.proposed: replica tower built 1991-92 (the 1877 iron tower was removed in 1929)
corrections.why: The 1877 iron tower was removed in 1929 and went to Lake Ontario as East Charity Shoal Light. The tower standing now is a 1991-92 replica. The 5.0 m height matches neither the 1877 tower (34 ft, about 10.4 m) nor the replica.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive's 1847 is the year the first (wooden) beacon was established on the pier. Wikidata's 1992 is the first lighting of the replica. Both are right for different structures; the historic light's first year is 1847.

notes_for_editor: 1) Height disputes: (a) the 1929 skeletal steel tower is 'ten-foot' in LighthouseFriends but 18 ft in Wikipedia (not cited in the story); (b) the 1991-92 replica is 'sixteen-foot' in one passage of LighthouseFriends but 34 ft in Wikipedia, and LighthouseFriends gives the 1877 original as 34 ft. The story gives no heights for these. Check on site or with the city before publication. 2) The record's structure (tower built 1877, 5.0 m, standing) is wrong for the present tower; proposed correction given. 3) Roster: matched to the USLHS 'Vermilion Pierhead' (historic pier light, est. 1847, 'not existing'), not the 'Vermilion (Replica)' record, which has no roster. The story treats the pierhead roster as this light's roster; Olin W. Stevens is from LighthouseFriends only and has no archive slug. 4) LighthouseFriends-only facts (flagged): the 1847 $3,000 appropriation, the 1858 inspection, the 1859 rebuild, the 1870-71 dwelling purchase, the 1877 cannon-iron source, the 1880 change to fixed red, the 1906 oil shed and walk, the 1929 removal, 1934 range lights, 1935 East Charity Shoal, and the 1991-92 campaign. The corpus Light-House Board volumes start in 1891, so pre-1891 items cannot be checked in primary text here. 5) Primary-checked: the 27 April 1893 collision (Board report, scan p. 192; OCR reads 'M. 8. Bacon'); the 1919 illuminant list (Bulletin 1919, PDF p. 39, read from the page image; see note 11), with the 2 September 1919 date from LighthouseFriends and the 1918-1923 index entry (change in illuminant). 6) Characteristic: LighthouseFriends gives a white flash every three seconds after the 1919 acetylene conversion and fixed red in its 2016 account. The story does not state the 1919-2016 characteristic; the editor should check the Coast Guard Light List. 7) The city of Vermilion web page returned no text; current status is from Main Street Vermilion (undated page). 8) Privacy: Ted Wakefield is named only for his public role in the fundraising campaign (LighthouseFriends). Olin W. Stevens is a keeper who died long ago; named for his public role. The keeper's dwelling is not named by its current business. 9) 'us-az-vermilion' (an Arizona replica in the record's related list) was not checked. 10) LighthouseFriends and Main Street Vermilion are paraphrased; the one quotation (a gallows frame standing on a completely wrecked pier) is a short phrase. 11) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1919 illuminant-change list on Bulletin PDF p.39 (printed p.95) was read from the page image: it reads Vermilion, Ohio, oil to acetylene, fixed red to flashing white. The OCR text layer merges that entry with the Ohio Light List line 'corrected to September 1, 1919'; the earlier draft quoted that merged phrase as the Bulletin's entry, and it is removed. The index entry 'Vermillion, change in illuminant 95' points to the same printed page. 12) The 1893 collision (Board report, scan p.192): OCR reads the tug as 'J. P. Derney' and 'J. F, Derney'; the name is given as J. P. Devney in LighthouseFriends, which the story uses. 13) The Board's 1893 entry is in the FY1893 report and says the plates were 'so badly injured that new plates had to be made'; the story now uses that wording. 14) LighthouseFriends dates the dwelling purchase to 1871 (the 1870 request is for a lot and dwelling); the story gives both dates as LighthouseFriends gives them.
